AIUP: Large US companies chosen and managed with the help of artificial intelligence models, heavily weighted to technology at about 70 percent. The AI-driven stock picking sets it apart from human-managed funds, aiming to spot patterns in data that people might miss.
BNGE: Streaming and gaming companies: the services that beam shows and games to screens, plus game makers and betting platforms, mostly communication firms. It is a focused bet on entertainment moving online, so it rides hits, subscribers and screen time.
BSJY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk kind, that all mature in 2034, so the fund ends like a single bond. It pays higher interest than safer bond funds in exchange for more default risk, aimed at a goal in the mid 2030s.
CBOA: Bitcoin with a built-in shock absorber: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while keeping gains only up to a cap. The trade is steadier bitcoin exposure in exchange for giving up the biggest rallies.
CBOY: Bitcoin exposure with the roughest swings softened: over each roughly one-year period starting in July, it seeks to protect against bitcoin's losses while following gains only up to a cap. It suits investors who want bitcoin in a portfolio without its full plunge risk.
CBXA: Bitcoin with a partial shield: over each roughly one-year period starting in April, it aims to absorb losses beyond the first 10 percent while following gains only up to a cap. It softens deep falls while leaving smaller dips with the investor.
DGJA: US large-company stocks wrapped in options set to pay a preset digital return if the market ends the year starting in January roughly flat or higher. The first slice of losses is buffered, trading away some upside for a more predictable result.
DGJL: Large US stocks paired with options designed to pay a preset digital return when the market finishes the year starting in July at least roughly flat. A buffer absorbs the first slice of any fall, so results are steadier but big rallies are mostly given up.
DGOC: Large US stocks with a twist: options are set so the fund aims to pay a preset digital return when the market ends the year starting in October roughly flat or up. A buffer softens the first slice of losses, but deep falls still hurt.
DYLG: The 30 blue-chip companies of the Dow, paired with call options sold on part of the portfolio for extra income. Selling only some calls leaves room to grow, so it balances payouts and upside better than a fully covered strategy, while still trimming big rallies.
EHY: Ether, the second-biggest cryptocurrency, paired with an aggressive covered call strategy that sells options on ether funds for high income. It keeps some of ether's upside while paying out option premiums, though the selling caps gains when ether runs hard.
EKG: Digital health companies: firms bringing software, connected devices and online services to medicine, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on health care going digital, from remote monitoring to virtual visits, and swings with that young industry.
EPMB: Mid-sized US companies across industries like industrial equipment, technology and business services, spread widely so no single stock dominates. It is a core holding for the middle of the market, aiming for steadier growth than small companies with more room to run than the biggest firms.
FLSA: Saudi Arabian companies, large and mid-sized, led by banks at over 40 percent with materials and energy firms behind. It is a single-country bet on the kingdom's economy and its push beyond oil, with extra political and currency risk.
FPXE: Recently listed European companies: the 100 largest and most tradable new stock market debuts and spin-offs across the continent. It is a bet on young public companies, led by health care and banks, so it carries the extra swing of fresh listings.
GEND: Dividend-paying US companies in a focused portfolio of a few dozen stocks, spread across health care, banks, energy and industrials. It is built for steady income from established payers, favoring reliable dividends over fast growth or the very highest yields.
GENW: Dividend-paying companies from outside the US, a focused list of a few dozen stocks led by banks at a bit over a third. It is built for income from abroad, favoring established payers over growth names, so it tilts toward value.
GOVM: US Treasury bonds maturing over the next one to ten years, all backed by the federal government. It is a middle-ground bond holding: steadier interest than cash-like funds, with prices that dip when interest rates climb.
GXLC: The 500 largest US companies in one fund, covering every major industry, with technology the biggest slice at about 40 percent. It works as a core holding that mirrors the broad US market, similar in spirit to S&P 500 funds.
HQGO: Large US growth companies screened for quality: strong, dependable businesses led by technology at a bit under half the fund. It aims for growth with a steadier foundation than go-go growth funds, holding profitable leaders rather than speculative names.
ISHP: Online shopping companies from around the world: retailers and marketplaces are the biggest slice, with media, delivery and technology firms behind them. It is a growth bet on buying moving online for good, spread across countries rather than one market.
IVSX: Small and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside North America, led by industrials at about a third. Managers apply a valuation approach, hunting for firms priced below what their cash flows suggest, so it is a value-tilted way to own smaller foreign stocks.
JOJO: A bond fund that rotates between riskier corporate credit in calm times and safer ground when its signals flash warning. The switching sets it apart from buy-and-hold bond funds, aiming to dodge credit blowups, though the calls can be wrong.
LIAM: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, known as TIPS, arranged to pay a steady income that keeps pace with inflation through 2055. It is built for very long horizons, funding later-life spending with payments designed not to lose buying power over the decades.
MAAY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to MARA, a bitcoin mining company, built to harvest its huge price swings as payouts. It is a high-risk trade: leverage resets and capped gains mean a crypto downturn can produce steep losses.
MBBB: Corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest investment-grade tier, screened with Moody's analytics to favor issuers less likely to be downgraded. They pay more than top-rated bonds, and the quality screen sets it apart from plain BBB funds that buy the whole tier.
MSST: An options strategy built around MicroStrategy, the company famous for holding huge amounts of bitcoin, aiming for income at a target 25 percent yearly rate. Its payouts ride on one of the market's wildest stocks, so the price can swing violently.
MUNF: Tax-exempt municipal bonds in a ladder stretching to 2036, paying federal-tax-free interest in regular distributions as bonds mature along the way. The long ladder suits savers funding spending in the mid 2030s who want income without the tax bite.
MUNJ: Tax-exempt municipal bonds arranged in a ladder ending around 2031, paying interest free of regular federal income tax along the way. It is designed to hand money back in stages for planned spending, rather than locking everything into one maturity date.
MYHA: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk-rated kind, bundled so they come due around 2027. The near end date makes it work like a single short bond: higher interest than safer funds, with principal due back soon if issuers stay healthy.
MYHB: Riskier corporate bonds rated below investment grade, grouped so that nearly all of them mature in 2028. It behaves like one junk bond with a set finish line, paying extra interest to compensate for the higher chance some issuers fail.
MYHC: High yield corporate bonds, rated below investment grade, that nearly all come due in 2029. Maturing together gives it a set end date like a single bond, paying higher interest in exchange for the risk that some issuers cannot pay.
MYHF: Junk-rated corporate bonds, the high yield kind, bundled so nearly all of them mature in 2032. The shared end date makes it act like a single bond with higher interest, built for a goal in the early 2030s if issuers hold up.
MYML: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that come due around 2032, paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax. The shared maturity makes it act like a single tax-free bond, handy for planning a goal in the early 2030s.
NFLP: An income strategy wrapped around Netflix stock, selling options to turn the streamer's price swings into regular payouts. It keeps some exposure if Netflix rises, but option selling caps the gains, and a sharp drop in the stock still hurts.
NLSI: A long-short stock strategy: it owns US companies it likes and bets against ones it does not, across technology, banks and energy, while selling options for income. The short side can soften market falls, though wrong bets on either side drag results.
NVIR: Energy companies plus the firms that clean up after the industry: drillers and producers alongside businesses that remediate old oil and gas sites. It is an actively managed bet that carbon energy stays essential while its cleanup becomes a business of its own.
OCTI: Developed-market stocks outside the US, wrapped in options that absorb the first 15 percent of losses over a one-year period starting in October. Gains are left uncapped, unusual for buffer funds, though the cushion is only measured when the period ends.
ODHY: High yield corporate bonds, the riskier junk kind, chosen with a defensive slant that favors sturdier borrowers over the highest payouts. It aims for bond income with fewer blowups than typical junk funds, though defaults and price swings still come with the territory.
PMAP: Large US stocks matching the S&P 500 mix, paired with an options cushion over the one-year period starting in April. It trades some upside for protection: gains stop at a cap, while the first slice of any market fall is absorbed.
PMNV: The broad US stock market through S&P 500 companies, wrapped in options that cushion the opening slice of a fall over the year starting in November. Because gains are capped, it is built for investors who want to stay in stocks with a softer landing.
PQX: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses, with the protection resetting every quarter instead of once a year. The shorter cycle keeps the cushion fresh, in exchange for capped gains each quarter.
RTYY: An income strategy using derivatives on a leveraged fund tied to Riot Platforms, a bitcoin mining company, converting its wild swings into payouts. It is a very risky trade: the leverage resets and options cap gains, so a crypto slump can hit hard.
TLA: A note-like bet on Tesla stock built from derivatives rather than shares, designed to pay income while the stock holds up or climbs. If Tesla drops hard, the fund can fall steeply with it, and its gains come with a ceiling.
UNHW: A weekly-reset strategy on UnitedHealth, the big US health insurer, aiming for about 1.2 times its weekly return plus weekly cash payouts. The weekly reset and slight leverage make it a short-term trading tool, far jumpier than simply holding the stock.
VMAX: Large US companies that look cheap for their earnings and assets, led by banks at about a third of the fund. It is a classic value holding: profitable, out-of-favor big names that can lag for stretches when growth stocks are fashionable.
WDNA: Companies in the genetics and biology revolution: gene editing, DNA sequencing and new drug discovery firms make up nearly the whole fund. It is a bet on biology becoming a technology industry, so it swings on research breakthroughs and trial results.
WTMY: Municipal bonds of many different maturities arranged in a ladder, chosen for high tax-free income. Interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, and the ladder spreads maturity risk, though the high income focus means some bonds are lower quality.
XEML: Europe's leading companies: drug makers, luxury goods houses, semiconductor equipment makers and industrial giants from across the continent. It gives diversified European exposure in one fund, though returns for US buyers also ride on currency moves between the euro and the dollar.
XTR: The 500 big US companies of the S&P 500, plus protective put options that gain value when the market crashes. The puts cost a little performance in calm years, so it is stocks with built-in crash insurance for worried investors.
